issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Exposed to Others' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure in this profile. It implies a visible, externally legible stigma or mark of trauma, but the rest of the profile does not include appearance-related injury, shame, or social-evaluative threat that would make this appraisal clinically coherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is not impossible after a toxic exposure, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation because no other item suggests a preventable omission, responsibility for others, or a scenario where the patient had a realistic chance to stop the event. In this profile it reads as insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is a weak fit to the trauma type and to the rest of the selected items. Loud or unexpected sounds are not a natural trigger/threat cue for toxic chemical exposure unless the trauma involved explosions, alarms, or similarly salient auditory signals, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a 76-year-old male with trauma from toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' is the least coherent item in the profile. Toxic chemical exposure more plausibly yields themes of bodily damage, contamination, helplessness, or mistrust of the body/environment. Severe guilt about not preventing the event can occur, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile: there are no memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting a role in causing the incident, failing to rescue others, or making a consequential decision. The other appraisal items are strongly body-focused and fit the trauma type well, making this guilt item stand out as insufficiently integrated with the formulation and surrounding content. The remaining items are clinically coherent with one another and with the active formulation pattern, especially the strong links among memory, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies.

vignette: Thomas, a 76-year-old hotel manager from a small town in the Midwest, had spent his career running the daily operations of a boutique resort on the lake. When a faulty ventilation system in the banquet hall released a toxic chemical plume of acrylonitrile during a busy wedding reception, he was among the first to notice the acrid stench and the sudden sharpness in his throat. The chemical seeped into his lungs, and a wave of panic surged through him, leaving his heart pounding and his hands trembling. He was rushed to the hospital, where physicians confirmed a high level of exposure and the presence of chemical burns on his skin and eyes. The event was brief yet searing, and it left a lingering impression that would shape the years that followed. In the weeks after the incident, Thomas found that the memory of the gas leak did not come as a single, coherent image. Instead, fragments of the scene appeared in a disjointed collage: the hiss of the ventilation duct, the flash of yellow warning lights, the sudden, almost involuntary cough, and the faint, chemical taste that lingered in his mouth. Whenever he caught a glimpse of a bright light or a sudden noise-whether a radio blaring a new song or the creak of the old wooden floorboards-his mind would flash back to that moment of choking and burning. The emotional intensity of the recollections was overwhelming, yet the mind offered no clear picture; it was a flood of feeling without a visible picture. That same intensity pushed him to put on loud music or turn on the television as soon as he could, hoping that the blaring volume would drown out the intrusive sensory echoes. He also began to monitor his thoughts constantly, searching for any sign that he was "going crazy" or losing his grip. The restaurant kitchen, where the leak had started, became a place he avoided altogether. He could not bear the thought of walking past the hallway that led to the banquet room, because even the memory of the smell of acrylonitrile would seep in through the vents. These sensory distractions and thought-monitoring tactics, while offering temporary relief, made the sense of threat grow sharper each time he experienced them. The persistent sense of danger that the memory stirred kept Thomas in a constant state of alert. At home he felt the need to check every door, every window, as if an invisible threat could burst through any crack. He could only find solace in a few isolated rooms-his bedroom, the small office behind the front desk-where he could lock the doors and feel a brief, fragile sense of safety. Even the sound of a phone buzzing on the kitchen counter or the hum of the old refrigerator could trigger a surge of anxiety; he would instinctively cover his ears or turn the volume up so high that the music drowned out the noise. This heightened threat perception led him to re-experience the fragmented recollections more frequently. Every unexpected sound became a cue that the chemical might return, and with each cue came another fragment of the original event, a new burst of terror, a sharper belief that his body was betraying him. He began to view his own physiological reactions-his racing heart, his tremors, the way his body would tense in response to any sudden noise-as evidence that his body was an enemy, perpetually primed for danger. The belief that he could not trust his own body, that his health was unreliable, made the threat feel all the more real. Because Thomas's sense of threat was now amplified by his own negative thoughts about his body, he felt perpetually unsafe. The belief that he could not rely on his body to protect him convinced him that every corner of the house, every sound, could signal another attack. The constant use of sensory distraction and thought monitoring, instead of helping him feel calm, began to erode his confidence in his own judgments. Each time he tuned out the music and heard a sudden clatter, he would remember that he had felt the same way during the chemical leak. That recollection, in turn, fed back into his fear that his body was unreliable, that he was helpless to prevent future harm. The more he relied on the distracting noise to escape, the more his body's natural responses-its own way of signaling danger-felt alien and untrustworthy. In the last year, Thomas's avoidance had started to impact his job. He no longer allowed guests to walk through the corridor leading to the banquet hall, which strained his relationship with the front-desk staff and the catering team. He would feel a tightness in his chest whenever a guest approached, and the constant urge to keep the lights on, the music blasting, left him exhausted. When he finally asked a colleague to take over a shift, he discovered that he could no longer focus on the tasks at hand, and the stress of his own internal alarm pushed him to the brink of leaving the hotel entirely. It was the cumulative weight of these experiences-an unrelenting sense of danger, a fractured memory that would not let go, a body he could not trust-that pushed Thomas to seek help. He was afraid that if he did not find a way to break the loop, his health would decline and he would lose his ability to manage the hotel he had spent a lifetime building. At the same time, he hoped that a therapist could help him learn to trust his body again and reclaim the quiet safety he once knew in his own home.
